title: Role of the HCM
tagline: One week as the HCM. Hiring, pay, changes, leave, costing, students, and records, all at once.
briefing: Morning. It's Monday, Oct 19, and you're the HCM for the Office of Learning Operations. This week, everything lands at once: hiring, pay, changes, leave, costing, students, and records.

Three payroll calendars run this week, and the right one depends on the worker. Exempt staff are paid monthly, and October's cutoff passed on the 18th. Hourly staff are paid weekly or biweekly: backdated changes close Wednesday, other changes Friday at 5:00 PM, and time cards are due Monday at noon.

Your job: get every request to the right outcome, through the right person, before its deadline. Managers own their team's time and approvals. Central HR, payroll, and your EC own theirs. You make sure it all lands.
Requests and quick questions arrive all week. Some are urgent; some are noise. On pay day, Friday Oct 30, you'll see what every decision did.

payday.clean: Clean pay day. Nobody at your desk with a pay stub. That is what good payroll support looks like: nothing happens.
payday.problems: Some problems reached people's paychecks. Let's trace each one back to the decision that caused it.

noise.subject: Lunch and learn moved to next Wednesday
noise.body: The November lunch and learn moved to next Wednesday at noon. No action needed.

noise.subject: Garage resurfacing next Monday
noise.body: The staff garage closes next Monday morning for resurfacing. Plan for the overflow lot.

noise.subject: Printer is jammed again
noise.body: The second floor printer is jammed. I put a sign on it.

steps.title: Read the payroll calendar

opener.speaker: coach
opener.line: Three payroll calendars run this week, and the one that applies depends on the worker. Before you open anything, walk me through them.

steps.context: Renee taps the 2026 payroll calendars pinned to the bulletin board: monthly for exempt staff, and biweekly and weekly for hourly staff.

attachment.title: 2026 Payroll Calendars, week of Oct 19
lines: Monthly (exempt staff and faculty): October HCM transaction cutoff was Sun Oct 18. Next cutoff Wed Nov 18.
Biweekly (hourly): pay period 22, Sun Oct 11 to Sat Oct 24.
Biweekly: Retro Change Cutoff Wed Oct 21. HCM transaction cutoff Fri Oct 23.
Weekly (hourly): Sun Oct 18 to Sat Oct 24. HCM transaction cutoff Fri Oct 23.
Biweekly and weekly time cards due Mon Oct 26 at noon. Paychecks Fri Oct 30.

steps.hint: Which calendar pays this worker? Start there, then find the cutoff on that calendar.

decisions.label: Hourly staff
decisions.prompt: Which is right for hourly staff paid biweekly?

choices.text: This period's changes close Friday at 5:00 PM, and time cards Monday at noon
choices.feedback: Right. A change effective this period, like a new hire or a schedule change, closes at Friday's HCM transaction cutoff, before the period even ends. Time cards close Monday at noon, then payroll signs off. Next time: put every cutoff on your calendar at the start of each period.

choices.text: This period's changes and time cards both close Monday at noon, at sign off
choices.feedback: Time cards are due Monday at noon, but changes close earlier, at Friday's HCM transaction cutoff. A change entered Monday misses this payroll. Next time: check each cutoff on the payroll calendar.

choices.text: Nothing closes until the checks go out on Oct 30, so this week's changes can wait
choices.feedback: The paycheck date is when people see the result. By then payroll has already run, and anything entered next week waits for the next payroll. Next time: work back from the cutoffs, not the paycheck date.

decisions.label: Jordan's raise
decisions.prompt: Marcus says Jordan's raise is coming this week, backdated to September. Which cutoff does it have to beat?

choices.text: Wednesday's Retro Change Cutoff, because the raise is backdated
choices.feedback: Backdated changes are retro changes. The Retro Change Cutoff comes about two business days before the HCM transaction cutoff, so payroll has time to recalculate the periods already paid. Next time: when the effective date falls in a paid period, plan for the earlier cutoff.

choices.text: Friday's 5:00 PM HCM transaction cutoff, like any other change
choices.feedback: Friday's cutoff is for changes effective this period. A raise backdated to a period that's already been paid is a retro change, and the Retro Change Cutoff is Wednesday. Next time: check the effective date first, then pick the cutoff.

choices.text: Any time. Retro pay catches up on backdated changes whenever they land
choices.feedback: Retro does pay the difference, but only in a payroll after the change is approved. Miss Wednesday's Retro Change Cutoff, and the back pay waits for the next payroll. Next time: backdated changes have the earliest cutoff of the period.

decisions.label: Dana's adjustment
decisions.prompt: Dr. Park gave final approval this morning to Dana's equity adjustment, effective Oct 1. Dana is exempt. When will it pay?

choices.text: In November's monthly payroll, with retro pay for October
choices.feedback: Exempt staff are paid monthly, and October's monthly cutoff was Sun Oct 18. A change approved after the cutoff pays in the next monthly payroll, with retro for the month it missed. Next time: find the worker's calendar before you promise a date.

choices.text: On Oct 30, since it was approved before Friday's 5:00 PM cutoff
choices.feedback: Friday's 5:00 PM cutoff is for the biweekly and weekly payrolls. Dana is paid monthly, and October's monthly cutoff passed on the 18th, so the adjustment pays in November with retro. Next time: match the worker to their calendar before you promise a date.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: You said my adjustment would be on this check. It isn't, and I'd already planned around it.
consequences.summary: Dana was promised the wrong pay date for her equity adjustment.

choices.text: From Nov 1 only, since October's cutoff passed and October is lost
choices.feedback: A missed cutoff delays pay; it doesn't erase it. The adjustment is effective Oct 1, so November's payroll pays it with retro for October. Next time: tell people when it pays, and that retro covers the gap.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: Compensation says October isn't lost at all. It comes as retro in November. Why did you tell me it was?
consequences.summary: Dana was told her October pay was lost and took it to Compensation.

steps.title: Access for a visiting evaluator
steps.context: A partner foundation is sending an evaluator to observe Dr. Park's fall workshops for six weeks. The foundation pays her. The office will not.

opener.speaker: dir_park
opener.line: Our evaluator needs Oracle access while she's here. How do we set her up?

steps.hint: Which setup is built for people the office never pays, and what does that setup leave out?

decisions.prompt: How do you set up the evaluator in Oracle?

choices.text: Non-worker with Active no payroll, left off the new hire report
choices.feedback: A non-worker with the Non-employment reason and Active no payroll gets access without pay, and only paid hires go on the new hire report. She needs a background check, but not an I-9. Next time: use the same setup for observers, contractors, and other unpaid affiliates.

choices.text: Staff hire with Active no payroll, so she has a record but no pay
choices.feedback: A staff hire makes her an employee, which brings an I-9 and the new hire report, for someone the office doesn't pay. Next time: set up unpaid people who need access as non-workers.

choices.text: Non-worker with Active no payroll, included on the new hire report
choices.feedback: The new hire report is for paid hires, so observers, contractors, and other affiliates are left off it. Next time: exclude unpaid affiliates from the new hire report.

steps.title: Can Noor start Wednesday?
steps.context: Marcus Bell is hiring Noor Haddad as a Program Assistant. Her background check is still pending, and she is not in your Pending Workers list yet.

opener.speaker: mgr_bell
opener.line: Noor accepted! Can she start Wednesday? We'll do the paperwork after.

steps.hint: What has to arrive before anyone can start work here, and what do you do once it comes?

decisions.prompt: Noor's background check is still pending, and she isn't converted. What do you tell Marcus?

choices.text: She can start once PCB sends clear to start and I convert her, so plan on Mon Oct 26
choices.feedback: No one starts work until PCB sends clear to start and you convert her, because that is what gives her a hire record, a time card, and pay. Next time: give the manager that rule and a realistic first day as soon as the offer is accepted.

choices.text: Yes to Wednesday, as long as she finishes the I-9 and hire paperwork by Friday
choices.feedback: Noor would work with no hire record and before her check cleared, so those days have no time card and no pay. I-9 Section 1 is due by the first day of work, so the paperwork can't come after. Next time: no one starts until clear to start and conversion, and the I-9 starts on day one.

consequences.speaker: new_haddad
consequences.line: I worked Wednesday through Friday before my official start, and none of it was on a time card. Am I getting paid for those days?
consequences.summary: Noor worked three days with no hire record, so the hours missed payroll and her I-9 was late.
consequences.task: Work with payroll to pay Noor for Oct 21 to 23, and complete her I-9 with the day she actually started.

choices.text: Have her come in Wednesday to shadow the team, unpaid, until her clear to start comes
choices.feedback: Shadowing the team is work, and work for the office has to be paid, whatever it's called. She'd also be on site before her background check cleared. Next time: there's no unpaid head start; she starts after clear to start and conversion.

consequences.speaker: new_haddad
consequences.line: Marcus asked me to come in and shadow before my start date, and I worked three full days. Nobody said that wasn't paid.
consequences.summary: Noor did three days of unpaid work before her check cleared, a wage and hour risk.
consequences.task: Work with payroll to pay Noor for the days she worked before her start date.

steps.title: Priya needs time off for her dad
steps.context: Priya Nair, an Event Specialist paid biweekly, stops by your desk. Dana Ortiz is her manager.

opener.speaker: emp_nair
opener.line: My dad has surgery next week and I'll be caring for him, so I may need days off, on and off, for a few weeks. What do I do?

steps.hint: Who decides whether a leave like this is protected, and what clock starts once the office hears about it?

decisions.label: Priya's request
decisions.prompt: What do you do with what Priya just told you?

choices.text: Get her request to Carmen on the leave team today, so she can hear her options
choices.feedback: Right. Caring for a parent after surgery can qualify for FMLA, and the leave team decides that, not you. Once the office knows an employee may need FMLA leave, the employer has 5 business days to send the eligibility notice, so the leave team needs it today. Next time: route any leave that might be protected the same day, and let the leave team handle the medical side.

consequences.speaker: emp_nair
consequences.line: Carmen called me the same day and walked me through everything before Dad's surgery. That was one less thing to worry about.
consequences.summary: Priya's leave reached the leave team on the first day.

choices.text: Ask about her dad's surgery and recovery first, so Carmen gets the full picture
choices.feedback: Her dad's diagnosis isn't yours to collect, and the leave team doesn't need you to gather it. The leave team handles eligibility and any medical certification directly, and the 5 business day notice clock keeps running while you ask questions. Next time: send the leave need to the leave team and keep medical questions out of it.

consequences.speaker: emp_nair
consequences.line: I didn't want to explain my dad's surgery at the HR desk. It felt like I had to prove he was sick enough.
consequences.summary: Priya was pressed for medical details the leave team didn't need.
consequences.task: Get Priya's leave need to the leave team, with no medical details.

choices.text: Have her plan the days with Dana and use PTO, since time off is Dana's call
choices.feedback: Dana approves everyday time off, but a leave that may be protected has to reach the leave team, and the employer's 5 business day clock for the eligibility notice started when the office heard about it. Handled as ordinary PTO, Priya can miss the notice and protection she's owed. Next time: let the manager plan the schedule, and send the leave need to the leave team the same day.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: Priya's been out twice this week for her dad, and I've been counting it as PTO. Nobody told me it might be FMLA.
consequences.summary: Priya's leave was handled as everyday time off, and the leave team heard about it too late for the FMLA notice.
consequences.task: Get Priya's leave need to the leave team and help Carmen catch up on the notice.

choices.text: No reply to Priya
choices.feedback: Priya's request sat unanswered, so the leave team never heard about it and the 5 business day notice window ran out. Next time: answer a leave request the day you get it and send it to the leave team.

consequences.speaker: leave_ruiz
consequences.line: Priya says she asked your office about leave on Oct 19 and never heard back. The notice deadline has passed.
consequences.summary: Priya's leave request went unanswered, and the FMLA notice deadline passed.

decisions.label: On and off days
decisions.prompt: Priya asks how her days off will count if the leave team approves on and off leave. How should her leave time be recorded?

choices.text: Record each absence as it happens, with the actual hours she's out
choices.feedback: Right. On and off leave is intermittent leave, so each absence is recorded on its date with the actual time taken. Only time actually taken counts against her 12 weeks. Next time: one block is for continuous leave; intermittent leave is recorded one occurrence at a time.

choices.text: Book one absence for the whole approval period, then trim it if she's back
choices.feedback: One long block counts the days she works as leave, so it overstates the time she has used and eats into her protection. Only time actually taken counts for intermittent leave. Next time: record intermittent leave per occurrence, with the actual time.

consequences.speaker: emp_nair
consequences.line: My leave record says I'm out for a whole month, but I've only missed two days. Am I using up my leave?
consequences.summary: Priya's on and off leave was booked as one block, overstating the time she used.
consequences.task: Correct Priya's leave record to the days she actually missed.

choices.text: Record nothing until her leave ends, then enter her total time off at once
choices.feedback: Waiting until the end means nothing tracks her protected time while she uses it, and days get lost. Each occurrence is recorded when it happens, with the actual time taken. Next time: record intermittent leave as it happens.

consequences.speaker: leave_ruiz
consequences.line: Priya was out two days this week and none of it is recorded. I can't track her protected time if it only shows up at the end.
consequences.summary: Priya's leave days went unrecorded as she took them.
consequences.task: Record Priya's leave days with the actual time taken.

decisions.label: Dana asks

spoken.speaker: mgr_ortiz
spoken.line: Priya says she'll need some time off next week. Is everything okay? What's going on with her?

decisions.prompt: Dana wants to know what's going on with Priya. What do you tell her?

choices.text: Say Priya may need some leave and you'll pass along dates as you get them
choices.feedback: Right. Dana needs to know Priya may be out and when, so she can plan coverage. The reason and any medical details stay with Priya and the leave team, and Priya can share more if she wants to. Next time: give managers dates and next steps, never health details.

choices.text: Tell her it's for her dad's surgery and recovery, so she can plan coverage
choices.feedback: Her dad's surgery is family medical information Priya shared to get help with leave. Dana can plan coverage with dates alone, so passing on the reason goes beyond what she needs. Next time: share that Priya may be out and when, and let Priya decide what else to tell.

consequences.speaker: emp_nair
consequences.line: Dana asked how my dad's surgery went in front of the whole team. I never told her about it.
consequences.summary: Priya's family medical details reached her manager without her okay.
consequences.task: Apologize to Priya and keep her leave details with the leave team.

choices.text: Tell her to ask Priya how serious the surgery is, so she can plan the coverage
choices.feedback: Sending Dana to ask about the surgery puts Priya on the spot about family medical details, and Dana can plan coverage with dates alone. Medical questions go through the leave team's certification process, not a manager's chat. Next time: give Dana the dates and next steps, and leave the medical side to the leave team.

consequences.speaker: emp_nair
consequences.line: Dana asked me what kind of surgery my dad is having before she'd okay my days off. I felt like I had to justify it.
consequences.summary: Dana pressed Priya for medical details on your advice.
consequences.task: Remind Dana that leave questions go to the leave team.

choices.text: No answer to Dana
choices.feedback: Dana didn't hear back, so she had to plan coverage without dates and ask Priya herself. Next time: answer the manager quickly with dates and next steps, and keep the medical details out of it.

steps.title: Dates for a resignation
steps.context: Dana Ortiz messages you in chat. She thinks someone on her team may resign soon and wants to know what you will need from her to enter it.

opener.speaker: mgr_ortiz
opener.line: If someone on my team resigns, which dates do you need from me?

steps.hint: A resignation has two key dates. What does each one mark?

decisions.prompt: Which dates do you ask Dana for?

choices.text: The day they told you, and their last day of work
choices.feedback: Right. The notification date is the day the employee told the manager, like the date on a resignation email, and the termination date is their last day of work. Next time: also ask for the last day worked if PTO covers the final days.

choices.text: Their last day of work, used for both dates
choices.feedback: The notification date is the day the employee told the manager, not the last day. Using one date for both erases the notice they gave and misstates the record. Next time: notification date is when they told you; termination date is the last day.

choices.text: Today's date, and the last day Oracle fills in
choices.feedback: Today is only the day you enter it, and Oracle may fill in a termination date from the notice period that is not their real last day. Next time: use the day they told the manager, and replace any filled in date with the actual last day.

steps.title: A gift card for Maya's event work
steps.context: Aisha Grant, who coordinates student help for the office's events, catches you in the break room. Maya Brooks, an undergraduate, worked 12 hours at last week's fall event, doing tasks Aisha assigned. The office has never hired Maya.

opener.speaker: emp_grant
opener.line: Maya worked 12 hours at the fall event and she was amazing. Can I just pay her with a $150 gift card from the event budget?

steps.hint: If Maya did work the office directed, what does that make her, and how does anyone in that role get paid?

decisions.label: Maya's 12 hours
decisions.prompt: Maya did 12 hours of work that Aisha directed. How should the office pay her?

choices.text: Hire her as a student worker so all 12 of her hours are paid through payroll
choices.feedback: Right. A student who does work the office directs is an employee, so her hours are wages paid through payroll, not a gift card. She worked before she was hired, so ask Ravi how to date the hire and pay those 12 hours. Next time: when someone wants to pay a student for work with a gift card, invoice, or stipend, hire the student.

choices.text: Approve the gift card as a thank you; 12 hours is a one time favor, not a job
choices.feedback: A gift card for hours worked is still pay for work, just outside payroll, with no taxes withheld and no record of her time. Calling it a thank you doesn't change what it pays for. Next time: when a student has worked, hire them and pay through payroll.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: There's a $150 gift card on the event budget for Maya. If it paid for her hours, that's wages outside payroll, and I can't book it as a thank you.
consequences.summary: Maya's 12 hours were paid with a gift card outside payroll, a wage and tax exposure.
consequences.task: Hire Maya as a student worker and pay her 12 hours through payroll.

choices.text: Set her up as Student Expense Only and reimburse the $150 as an expense
choices.feedback: Student Expense Only is for paying back a student's actual expenses when she has no paid role. Using it for 12 hours of work dresses up wages as an expense, with no I-9. Next time: pay for work goes through a student worker hire, never an expense setup.

consequences.speaker: ec_menon
consequences.line: Maya's Student Expense Only record paid her for 12 hours of work. That setup isn't for wages, and she has no I-9.
consequences.summary: Maya's wages were paid as an expense reimbursement, with no I-9.
consequences.task: Hire Maya as a student worker, complete her I-9, and fix the payment with payroll.

choices.text: Pay her a service free stipend for the event, since she isn't on staff
choices.feedback: A service free stipend is only for a student who performs no services, and Maya worked 12 hours. Using it for work creates an employee with no I-9, which is a compliance gap. Next time: if a student did the work, she's a student worker with an I-9.

consequences.speaker: ec_menon
consequences.line: Maya's record says service free stipend, but she worked 12 hours at the event. That's an employee with no I-9.
consequences.summary: Maya was set up as a service free stipend for work she did, so she has no I-9.
consequences.task: Hire Maya as a student worker and complete her I-9.

decisions.label: Maya's record
decisions.prompt: In Oracle, Maya has only an enrolled student (N) record. What do you add to set her up as a paid student worker?

choices.text: Add the employment Work Relationship to the person record she already has
choices.feedback: Right. With only an enrolled student (N) record, Maya has no employee relationship yet, so you add the employment Work Relationship to her existing person record. Her assignment then gets hire reason Hire employment, status Active payroll eligible, and an end date that matches her work. Next time: search first; the record that's there tells you which action to use.

choices.text: Add an assignment to her enrolled student record for the event work
choices.feedback: Add Assignment is for someone who already has an employee (E) assignment. Maya has only a student (N) record, so there's no employee relationship to add a job to. Next time: N record only means add the employment Work Relationship; an E assignment means add an assignment.

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: Maya's paid job is sitting under her student record, not an employee relationship. Payroll can't pay her hours like that.
consequences.summary: Maya's job was added under the wrong relationship, so her hours didn't pay.
consequences.task: Fix Maya's record with Ravi and add the employment Work Relationship.

choices.text: Create a new employee person record for her paid student job
choices.feedback: Oracle keeps one person record per person. A second record splits Maya's history and pay across two records that are hard to merge. Next time: search first and add the work relationship to the record she has.

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: Maya has two person records now, one as a student and one as an employee. We have to merge them before her pay is right.
consequences.summary: A duplicate person record was created for Maya.
consequences.task: Ask Ravi to help fix Maya's duplicate record.

choices.text: Not set up
choices.feedback: Maya was never set up, so there's no record to pay her hours from. Next time: set up the record the same week the hire is agreed.

consequences.speaker: stu_brooks
consequences.line: Aisha said I'd get paid for the event, but nobody ever set me up.
consequences.summary: Maya was never set up, so her 12 hours are still unpaid.

decisions.label: Maya's checks
decisions.prompt: Aisha wants Maya back for more events this fall. What does Maya's student worker hire need?

choices.text: An I-9, done right away, and no background check
choices.feedback: Right. Student workers need an I-9 but no background check. Section 1 is due by the first day of work for pay and Section 2 within 3 business days, so with work already done, complete it now and never backdate it. Next time: finish the hire before a student works a single hour.

choices.text: An I-9 and a background check, with clear to start from PCB
choices.feedback: Student workers need an I-9 only; background checks are for staff, faculty, and campus affiliates. Ordering one Maya doesn't need holds up her hire. Next time: check the worker type before you order checks.

consequences.speaker: emp_grant
consequences.line: Maya couldn't work this week's event because she was waiting on a background check. I thought student workers didn't need one.
consequences.summary: An unneeded background check held up Maya's hire.
consequences.task: Cancel the extra check and finish Maya's hire.

choices.text: No I-9, since she's enrolled and her student record already covers her
choices.feedback: Federal law requires an I-9 for every paid employee, students included, and a student record doesn't cover it. Paying her with no I-9 is a compliance gap. Next time: every student worker gets an I-9, with Section 2 done within 3 business days of the first day of work.

consequences.speaker: ec_menon
consequences.line: Maya has worked two events now with no I-9 on file. Every paid employee needs one, students too.
consequences.summary: Maya worked with no I-9, a federal compliance gap.
consequences.task: Complete Maya's I-9 now.

steps.title: A new Events Coordinator position
steps.context: Dr. Park approved budget for one new Events Coordinator on Dana Ortiz's team. Dana sent her notes before stopping by.

opener.speaker: mgr_ortiz
opener.line: I found our old Events Coordinator position from 2019. Can you switch it back on and get it posted this week?

attachment.title: From Dana: Events Coordinator
lines: Budget: approved by Dr. Park for 1 Events Coordinator
Hours: 30 a week, on site at our Nashville office
Old position I found: Events Coordinator, inactive since 2019
Job code on the old position: 4417
Category on the old position: Staff non-exempt

steps.hint: What could an old position carry into a new hire, and what does central HR need to see before it approves a staff position?

decisions.label: The 2019 position
decisions.prompt: Dana wants the inactive 2019 position switched back on and posted. What do you do?

choices.text: Ask Ravi to get Compensation's pre-search memo, then create a new position from it
choices.feedback: An inactive position can carry a retired job code that blocks approval. Central HR approves a new staff position only with Compensation's pre-search memo attached. Next time: get the memo through your EC first, then build a new position from its six-digit job code.

choices.text: Ask Ravi to refresh the 2019 description, then reactivate that position and post it
choices.feedback: The 2019 position carries a retired four-digit job code, so reactivating it can be blocked or sent back. Central HR also needs the pre-search memo before it approves a staff position. Next time: don't reactivate inactive positions; create a new one from the memo.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: Central HR sent the old Events Coordinator position back because of its job code. We lost two weeks, and there's still no posting.
consequences.summary: The reactivated 2019 position was sent back, and the search slipped two weeks.
consequences.task: Request the pre-search memo through Ravi and create a new position.

choices.text: Reactivate it, then update its job code from Compensation's pre-search memo
choices.feedback: Old job codes on an inactive position can block the update itself, and its old data would follow into the requisition and the hire. Next time: leave inactive positions alone, and create a new one from the pre-search memo.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: Central HR couldn't approve the update to the old position because of its retired job code. Now we're starting over with a new one.
consequences.summary: The update to the reactivated 2019 position was blocked, and the search slipped.
consequences.task: Create a new position from the pre-search memo.

choices.text: Nothing started by Wednesday
choices.feedback: No memo request and no position, so the Events Coordinator search didn't start this week. Next time: start the memo request through your EC the day a new role is approved.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: I asked about the Events Coordinator role on Monday. A week later, nothing has been requested.
consequences.summary: The Events Coordinator search never started.
consequences.task: Request the pre-search memo through Ravi.

decisions.label: Hours
decisions.prompt: The role is 30 hours a week. How do you set the hours on the position?

choices.text: Standard working hours 40, and working hours 30
choices.feedback: Standard working hours stay at 40 so the FTE calculates correctly: 30 of 40 is 0.75. Getting this wrong is the most common position error, and it follows the hire into pay and reports. Next time: Standard 40 every time, with the real hours in Working hours.

choices.text: Standard working hours 30 to match the role, and working hours 30
choices.feedback: Typing 30 into Standard working hours makes the FTE 1.0, so a 30-hour role reads as full time in the budget and in reports. Next time: keep Standard at 40, and put the actual 30 in Working hours.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: The Events Coordinator position shows 1.0 FTE. I budgeted 0.75 for it, so my numbers don't match.
consequences.summary: The position was built at 1.0 FTE instead of 0.75.
consequences.task: Update the position: Standard working hours 40, working hours 30.

choices.text: Standard working hours 40, working hours 40, and override to 30 at hire
choices.feedback: The position would read as full time, so the requisition and the offer would carry 40 hours for a 30-hour role, whatever you override later. Next time: put the real hours in Working hours on the position, with Standard at 40.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: The Events Coordinator position says 40 hours a week. If it posts that way, candidates will expect a full-time job.
consequences.summary: The position was built at 40 hours instead of 30.
consequences.task: Update the position's working hours to 30 before the requisition is created.

choices.text: Not entered
choices.feedback: No position was built, so no hours were set. Next time: build the position as soon as the pre-search memo arrives.

decisions.label: Requisition
decisions.prompt: Once the position is approved, Dana wants the requisition open for "two or three, in case we like more than one." How do you set it up?

choices.text: Limited, 1 opening, with the Nashville office as the primary location
choices.feedback: The recruiting partner bills for every opening, so you open exactly the seats you have budget for, at the real location. Next time: Limited with the exact number, and a specific site, never United States.

choices.text: Limited, 3 openings, with the Nashville office as the primary location
choices.feedback: Three openings for one budgeted seat means paying for two openings you'll never fill, and canceling them costs half the fee. Next time: Limited, with the exact number of seats you have budget for.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: There's a recruiting charge for three Events Coordinator openings. We have budget for one.
consequences.summary: Two extra openings were billed to the department.
consequences.task: Ask central recruiting to close the two extra openings.

choices.text: Unlimited openings, with United States as the primary location
choices.feedback: Unlimited is never used, since every opening is billed, and United States hides whether the job is in a state that requires a posted pay range. Next time: Limited with the exact seats, and the specific location.

consequences.speaker: rec_nguyen
consequences.line: The Events Coordinator requisition came in as Unlimited with a United States location. I sent it back, so the posting slipped a week.
consequences.summary: The requisition was sent back for unlimited openings and a vague location.
consequences.task: Resubmit the requisition with 1 opening and the Nashville office as the location.

choices.text: Not entered
choices.feedback: The requisition wasn't set up, so the search didn't start. Next time: set it up as soon as the position is approved.

steps.title: Kai shows two assignments
steps.context: Dana Ortiz is looking at Kai Brennan's record. It lists his job in your office and a part-time teaching job in the School of Education, with a manager she doesn't know.

opener.speaker: mgr_ortiz
opener.line: Kai's record shows a second job with some other manager. Is that a mistake we should fix?

steps.hint: Where does a manager live in Oracle: on the person, or somewhere more specific?

decisions.prompt: What do you tell Dana about Kai's second job?

choices.text: Leave it, since the teaching job is its own assignment with its own manager
choices.feedback: Right. One person can hold more than one assignment, and each one carries its own job, department, manager, hours, and pay. Kai's teaching job belongs to the School of Education. Next time: check which assignment you are on before you act.

choices.text: Change that assignment's manager to Dana, so it matches his job here
choices.feedback: The manager lives on each assignment, not on the person. Kai reports to Dana for his job here, but his teaching job has its own manager in another school, and that record isn't yours to change. Next time: act only on the assignment in your area.

choices.text: Ask the EC to end the extra assignment, since it looks like a leftover
choices.feedback: Nothing is left over, so there is nothing for the EC to fix. Two jobs mean two assignments, and ending the teaching one would stop pay for work Kai still does. Next time: read the assignment details before you call something a mistake.

steps.title: Mei's Friday off
steps.context: Mei Chen, the office's Budget Analyst, is exempt and paid monthly. She's taking Fri Oct 23 off, and Dana Ortiz approves her time off.

opener.speaker: emp_chen
opener.line: I'm taking this Friday off. Can you put it on the time card system for me, like everyone else's?

steps.hint: What does Mei's pay type tell you about where her time off belongs, and who has to act before it counts?

decisions.label: Where it goes
decisions.prompt: Mei wants her Friday off on the time card system. What do you do?

choices.text: Enter it in Oracle with Add Absence, after a look at her balance
choices.feedback: Right. Exempt time off lives in Oracle absences; the time card system is for non-exempt staff. Check Absence Balance and Existing Absences first, then use Add Absence with the right type and date. Next time: check exempt status before you enter any time off.

choices.text: Add a PTO row to her time card before time cards are due Monday at noon
choices.feedback: The time card system holds non-exempt time. Mei is exempt, so her time off belongs in Oracle absences, and a time card row puts it in the wrong system with the wrong balance. Next time: exempt time off goes in Oracle with Add Absence; non-exempt time off goes on the time card.

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: Mei is exempt, but her Friday off showed up on the time card system. It doesn't belong there, and her Oracle balance never changed.
consequences.summary: Mei's day off went into the wrong system, so her Oracle balance is wrong.
consequences.task: Remove the time card row and enter Mei's absence in Oracle.

choices.text: Email payroll the date so they can take the day off her balance
choices.feedback: Payroll doesn't enter absences; it pays from what's recorded. An email leaves no absence in Oracle, so nothing tracks Mei's day off. Next time: enter exempt time off with Add Absence, or have the employee enter it herself.

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: I got an email about Mei's Friday off, but payroll doesn't enter absences. Nothing was ever recorded.
consequences.summary: Mei's day off was emailed to payroll instead of entered, so it was never recorded.
consequences.task: Enter Mei's absence in Oracle with Add Absence.

choices.text: Tell her exempt staff don't record days off, so there's nothing to enter
choices.feedback: Exempt staff don't use time cards, but their time off is still recorded, in Oracle absences. Skipping it leaves her balance wrong and no record of the day. Next time: exempt time off goes in Oracle with Add Absence.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: Mei was out Friday and there's no absence on file. Her balance still shows that day.
consequences.summary: Mei's Friday off was never recorded.
consequences.task: Enter Mei's Friday absence in Oracle.

decisions.label: Approval
decisions.prompt: Once it's in Oracle, Mei's absence still shows Awaiting approval with Dana on Tuesday afternoon. What do you do?

choices.text: Ask Dana to approve it from her bell, then check it moves to Scheduled
choices.feedback: Right. Awaiting approval means it's still with Dana and hasn't reached payroll; once she approves, a future absence shows Scheduled. October's monthly cutoff passed Oct 18, so it needs approval before the Nov 18 cutoff to reach November's payroll. Next time: watch the bell after you submit, and chase approvers early instead of near the cutoff.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: My Friday off was approved before I left, and my balance is right. Easy.
consequences.summary: Mei's absence was approved and recorded correctly.

choices.text: Tell Mei it's done, since Dana will see it in her bell before Friday
choices.feedback: Submitted isn't approved, and a request in someone's bell can sit there for weeks. An absence waiting on an approver hasn't reached payroll, and it doesn't move until someone acts. Next time: check the status in Existing Absences and chase the approver.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: My Friday off still says Awaiting approval. Did it ever count, or do I still have that day?
consequences.summary: Mei's absence sat with Dana unapproved, so it never reached payroll.
consequences.task: Get Dana to approve Mei's absence before the Nov 18 cutoff.

choices.text: Enter Friday a second time so a fresh request lands in front of Dana today
choices.feedback: A second absence for the same day is a duplicate, and once both are approved it doubles her time off. To change or restart an absence, edit or withdraw the one that's there. Next time: never double enter; chase the approver instead.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: My balance went down two days for one Friday off.
consequences.summary: A duplicate absence doubled Mei's time off.
consequences.task: Withdraw Mei's duplicate absence.

choices.text: Add the day to her time card too, so payroll sees it either way
choices.feedback: Entering the day in two systems doesn't speed anything up. It puts an exempt absence where it doesn't belong and leaves the real one still waiting on Dana. Next time: one record, in Oracle, and chase the approver.

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: Mei's day off is in Oracle and on the time card system. She's exempt, so the time card entry has to come off.
consequences.summary: Mei's day off was entered twice, in two systems.
consequences.task: Remove the time card entry for Mei.

steps.title: Reimbursing a student's train fare
steps.context: Aisha, in chat: "She came to our forum as an invited guest. She has no job with us and isn't paid anything. She just wants her $80 back."

opener.speaker: emp_grant
opener.line: A student we invited to our forum paid $80 for her train ticket. How do we pay her back?

steps.hint: Is this student being paid for work, or only paid back for what she spent?

decisions.prompt: How should the student be set up for the reimbursement?

choices.text: Student Expense Only, with no I-9 or background check
choices.feedback: Right. A student who only needs expenses paid back, with no paid role, is Student Expense Only, with no I-9 and no background check. Its exact Oracle setup is still being confirmed, so check with Ravi before you enter it. Next time: decide the setup first; paying back expenses isn't pay for work.

choices.text: Hire her as a student worker so the $80 can run through payroll
choices.feedback: Hiring her treats a reimbursement like pay, and it creates an employment record and an I-9 for someone who does no paid work. Next time: student worker is for pay for work; a reimbursement with no paid role is Student Expense Only.

choices.text: Pay the $80 as a service free stipend, since she does no work for us
choices.feedback: A service free stipend is for a student who receives a stipend with no work attached. Paying back a train ticket is a reimbursement, not a stipend. Next time: a student who only needs expenses paid back is Student Expense Only.

steps.title: SSNs and salaries for the grant report
steps.context: Dr. Helen Park is preparing the Wellness grant report. The grant pays half of Lena Kowalski's salary. Her email asks for data on everyone in the office.

opener.speaker: dir_park
opener.line: Did you see my email? I need that spreadsheet for the grant report by noon tomorrow.

attachment.title: Wellness grant report
lines: From: Dr. Helen Park
To: You
Subject: Wellness grant report
Please email me a spreadsheet with every employee's name, Social Security number, and salary by noon Tuesday.
I need it for the Wellness grant report. Thanks!

steps.hint: If this spreadsheet landed in the wrong inbox, what would be in it?

decisions.label: What to send
decisions.prompt: Dr. Park wants SSNs and salaries for everyone, by email. What do you send her?

choices.text: Only what the report needs, by person number, after you confirm it
choices.feedback: Right. Access is not permission to share, and SSNs never go in email or spreadsheets, so they stay out whatever the report needs. The person number identifies each person, and Dr. Park gets what the grant report needs and nothing more. Next time: ask what the task needs, then send only that.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: The grant report went in on time, and nobody's Social Security number left this office. Good call.
consequences.summary: The grant report was filed without exposing anyone's SSN.

choices.text: Exactly the 3 columns she asked for, sent as a password-protected file
choices.feedback: A password protects the file, not the choice to put every SSN in it. Once it is opened, it can be forwarded, saved, and printed, and the grant report never needed SSNs. Next time: leave SSNs out and identify people by person number.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: I forwarded your file to the grant office with the password right below it. Now I'm told that's a data incident.
consequences.summary: The SSN spreadsheet left the office with its password, and a data incident was opened.
consequences.task: Report the incident and make sure every copy of the file is deleted [SME: incident reporting contact].

choices.text: Check the email is really from her, then send the 3 columns as asked
choices.feedback: Checking who is asking is smart, but it doesn't change what belongs in the file. SSNs never go in email or spreadsheets, and even a director gets only what the task needs. Next time: confirm who is asking and why, then send the minimum, by person number.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: Dr. Park forwarded me the grant file to check the budget lines. Why do I have everyone's Social Security numbers?
consequences.summary: The SSN spreadsheet was forwarded to someone with no need for it.
consequences.task: Report the incident and make sure every copy of the file is deleted [SME: incident reporting contact].

choices.text: No reply by Tuesday noon
choices.feedback: Dr. Park heard nothing by noon, and the grant report stalled while she waited. Next time: answer the same day, and say what you can send instead.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: I asked for the grant data Monday and never heard back. I had to ask the funder for more time.
consequences.summary: The grant report was delayed waiting on data.

decisions.label: Building the list
decisions.prompt: No catalog or Playbook report has the columns the grant report needs. How do you build the list?

choices.text: Create an analysis with only the needed columns, then spot-check it
choices.feedback: Right. Start from the smallest set of columns that answers the question, then check a few people against Employment Info before you trust it. Save it in My Folders, where only you can see it [SME: which reporting roles HCMs have]. Next time: build something new only when no existing report fits.

choices.text: Create an analysis with every worker column, and hide the ones she doesn't need
choices.feedback: Hiding a column is not security. The data is still in the analysis and in anything exported from it, and access comes from Oracle roles, not from what you hide. Next time: leave out the columns you don't need.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: Dr. Park passed me your grant file, and the hidden columns had everyone's home address. I shouldn't be able to see that.
consequences.summary: Hidden columns in the grant file exposed personal data.

choices.text: Export the full roster report, then delete the extra columns in Excel
choices.feedback: A full export puts everyone's personal data on your computer, and trimming it by hand is easy to get wrong. Keep personal data in the system and pull only what the task needs. Next time: build the list with only the columns you need.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: Your grant file still had home addresses in a column way off to the right. I almost sent it to the funder.
consequences.summary: A hand-trimmed export missed a column of personal data.

choices.text: Nothing built by Tuesday noon
choices.feedback: No list was built, so the grant report waited. Next time: build the smallest list that answers the question and send it on time.

steps.title: Which title will the new hire get?
steps.context: Dana is drafting the Events Coordinator posting early. She wants the posting title to read Campus Events Coordinator, so candidates know what the job is.

opener.speaker: mgr_ortiz
opener.line: If we post it as Campus Events Coordinator, is that the title the new hire gets in Oracle?

steps.hint: What does a six-digit job code bring with it, besides a pay range?

decisions.prompt: What do you tell Dana about the title?

choices.text: No. Their business title will be the job name that comes with the job code
choices.feedback: The business title is the job name from the job architecture, which ends in its level, not the posting title or the position name. Next time: make the posting title clear for candidates, and expect the job name as the business title.

choices.text: No. Their business title will be the name we give the position itself
choices.feedback: The position name doesn't become the business title; the job name from the job architecture does. Next time: name positions clearly, but expect the business title to follow the job code.

choices.text: Yes. The requisition title carries over and becomes their business title
choices.feedback: The requisition title is only the posting title. The new hire's business title is the job name from the job architecture. Next time: tell managers the posting title is for candidates only.

steps.title: Sam's new title isn't showing
steps.context: Sam Okafor's business title still reads Receptionist, an old title that doesn't match his job name, Office Assistant 2. Last Thursday you submitted a Change Assignment at Dana Ortiz's request to fix it, but his Employment Info still shows Receptionist.

opener.speaker: mgr_ortiz
opener.line: Sam's new title still isn't showing. Did my change get lost, or should we just enter it again?

steps.hint: Before you redo anything, what would tell you where the first change is right now?

decisions.label: Finding the change
decisions.prompt: Where do you look first to see what happened to the change?

choices.text: Open the notifications bell and read the change's approval history
choices.feedback: Right. The bell shows each transaction's approval history: who approved, who it is waiting on, and any comments. This one has waited on Dr. Park since Thursday, and it isn't in the record until every approver acts [SME: approval chain for assignment changes]. Next time: check the bell daily and before every cutoff.

choices.text: Enter the title change again today, since the first one never posted
choices.feedback: The first change was never lost; it was waiting on an approver. A second one puts a duplicate in Dr. Park's queue, and if both are approved, Sam's record takes two updates. Next time: read the approval history in the bell before you redo anything.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: I had two identical title changes for Sam in my queue. Which one was I supposed to approve?
consequences.summary: A duplicate title change for Sam cluttered Dr. Park's approvals.
consequences.task: Withdraw the duplicate title change.

choices.text: Email payroll to ask whether the change reached them last week
choices.feedback: Payroll doesn't approve business title changes, and a pending change never reaches them. The answer was in the approval history, one click away. Next time: track your own transactions in the notifications bell.

consequences.speaker: emp_okafor
consequences.line: My new title still isn't on anything. Dana told me it was done last week.
consequences.summary: Sam's title change sat unapproved for another week while the wrong team was asked.

choices.text: No follow-up by noon
choices.feedback: Nobody checked the approval history, so the change kept waiting and Dana kept wondering. Next time: check the bell the same day someone asks.

consequences.speaker: mgr_ortiz
consequences.line: Sam's title still says Receptionist. Is anyone looking at this?
consequences.summary: Sam's title change was still waiting on approval at pay day.

decisions.label: The typo
decisions.prompt: The change is still waiting on Dr. Park, and the new title has a typo. What do you do?

spoken.speaker: mgr_ortiz
spoken.line: Hold on, it says Asistant, with one s. Can we fix that?

choices.text: Withdraw it, fix the typo, resubmit, and give Dr. Park a heads-up
choices.feedback: Right. While approval is in progress, the requester can withdraw a transaction, correct it, and resubmit. The approvals start over, so tell Dr. Park a corrected version is on its way [SME: on-screen label for withdraw]. Next time: read every field back against the source before you submit.

consequences.speaker: emp_okafor
consequences.line: My new title showed up, spelled right. Thanks for catching that.
consequences.summary: Sam's corrected title posted cleanly.

choices.text: Leave it with Dr. Park, and fix the typo once she approves it
choices.feedback: Once she approves, the typo becomes Sam's title of record and flows into every roster and the org chart until a second change fixes it. That's two transactions and two approvals for one change. Next time: withdraw and fix it while it's still pending.

consequences.speaker: emp_okafor
consequences.line: The org chart says I'm an Office Asistant 2. Can someone fix that before more people see it?
consequences.summary: Sam's title posted with a typo and showed up on the org chart.
consequences.task: Submit a correction for Sam's business title.

choices.text: Ask Dr. Park to reject it so you can submit it again
choices.feedback: Rejecting is the approver's tool, and asking for it puts your fix on Dr. Park's plate. While a change is pending, the requester can withdraw it, correct it, and resubmit. Next time: withdraw your own transaction when it needs a fix.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: You asked me to reject Sam's title change so you could fix a typo. You can pull those back yourself, can't you?
consequences.summary: Dr. Park was pulled in to reject a change the HCM could have withdrawn, and Sam's title waited longer.

steps.title: Rehiring a former program aide
steps.context: Marcus wants to bring back a program aide who left in 2023. Tyler Nguyen in central recruiting says her termination record shows No for rehire.

opener.speaker: mgr_bell
opener.line: She was great. Can't we just change that to Yes and make the offer?

steps.hint: Where did that No come from, and who has to look at it with you?

decisions.prompt: What do you tell Marcus?

choices.text: Hold any offer, and review the No with Tyler and Ravi before anyone commits
choices.feedback: A No means review comes before any offer, with the recruiter and your EC. Who can approve an exception is still being confirmed [SME]. Next time: check a former employee's rehire field before anyone promises a job.

choices.text: Ask Ravi to change her rehire field to Yes, since Marcus can vouch for her work

consequences.speaker: ec_menon
consequences.line: I was asked to flip a rehire field from No to Yes so an offer could go out. That needs a review, not an edit.

choices.text: Make the offer now, as long as it depends on Ravi clearing the No afterward

steps.title: Moving a team when a manager leaves
steps.context: Dr. Helen Park is planning ahead. The last time a manager left the office, that manager's team sat without an approver for weeks and time cards stalled.

opener.speaker: dir_park
opener.line: If one of my managers leaves, how do we move their whole team to someone new?

steps.hint: What happens to approvals while a team is still attached to someone who is gone?

decisions.prompt: What do you tell Dr. Park?

choices.text: Direct Reports on the manager, dated by their last day
choices.feedback: Direct Reports moves the whole team in one transaction from the manager's record, effective on or before the last day, so approvals never land on someone who is gone. Next time: move reports before the termination, and confirm the new manager's approver setup with your EC [SME].

choices.text: Direct Reports on the manager, once the termination is approved
choices.feedback: Waiting for the termination leaves the team attached to a manager who is gone, so approvals and time cards stall in the gap. Next time: move the team first, effective on or before the manager's last day.

choices.text: Terminate the manager first; the team moves up to you
choices.feedback: Reports don't move up on their own. Terminating first leaves them attached to someone who is gone, so approvals and time cards stall. Next time: move the team with Direct Reports before the termination.

steps.title: Aisha moves to 30 hours

opener.speaker: mgr_bell

attachment.title: Aisha's new schedule
lines: From: Marcus Bell
To: You
Subject: Aisha Grant, 30 hours a week
Aisha asked to go from 40 to 30 hours a week, and I approve.

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: I got your email about Aisha, but her record still says 40 hours. I can't change assignments; that has to come from you.
consequences.summary: Aisha's hours change was emailed to payroll instead of entered in Oracle.

choices.text: Not entered

decisions.label: Effective date

choices.text: Sun Oct 25

consequences.speaker: emp_grant
consequences.line: My new schedule started Sunday, and my record already shows 30 hours. That was painless.

choices.text: Mon Oct 26

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: Aisha's hours change starts on a Monday, one day into the period. Can you move it to Sunday so her record lines up with the pay period?
consequences.summary: Aisha's hours change was dated mid period and needs a correction.

choices.text: Sun Nov 1

consequences.speaker: mgr_bell
consequences.line: Aisha's been on 30 hours since Sunday, but her record says the change starts November 1. Which one is right?
consequences.summary: Aisha's hours change was dated a week late, in the middle of a pay period.

choices.text: Not entered by Friday's cutoff

consequences.speaker: mgr_bell

steps.title: Mei's home office payment

opener.speaker: mgr_ortiz
opener.line: Dr. Park approved a home office payment for Mei. She should take home exactly $500. How will you set it up?

steps.context: Dana asks in chat. Mei is exempt and paid monthly, and October's monthly cutoff passed on the 18th.
steps.hint: Is $500 what Mei takes home, or what she's paid before taxes? And which payroll month can it still make?

decisions.prompt: How do you set up the payment?

choices.text: Amount: $500, start date Nov 1
choices.feedback: Amount means gross, so taxes come out of the $500 and Mei takes home less than promised. Next time: use Net when the employee should take home an exact amount.

choices.text: Net: $500, start date Tue Oct 20

steps.title: An unpaid intern for data entry
steps.context: A student from a local college asked Dr. Helen Park about interning with the office this spring.

opener.speaker: dir_park
opener.line: Let's have her handle our regular data entry, 15 hours a week from January to May, unpaid. It's great experience for her, and it saves us budget.

steps.hint: In this setup, who gets the most out of it: the student or the office?

decisions.label: Paid or unpaid
decisions.prompt: Dr. Park wants the intern to do the office's regular data entry without pay. What do you tell her?

choices.text: Plan to pay her, since regular data entry is work the office would pay for
choices.feedback: An internship can be unpaid only when the intern, not the office, is the primary beneficiary. Doing the office's regular work points the other way. Next time: settle paid or unpaid before the start date, and when it's unclear, treat it as paid and ask your EC.

choices.text: Keep it unpaid if she earns course credit and signs a no-pay agreement
choices.feedback: A signed agreement doesn't change who benefits, and course credit is only one factor; no single factor decides the primary beneficiary test. An intern doing the office's regular work may legally be an employee, owed at least minimum wage and overtime. Next time: weigh the whole test, and treat regular work as paid work.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: Ravi says my unpaid internship could turn into a wage claim, even with credit and a waiver. I wish I'd known before I talked to the student.
consequences.summary: Dr. Park planned an unpaid internship for work that should be paid, a wage and hour risk.
consequences.task: Work with Ravi to make the internship a paid hire before January.

choices.text: Pay her a flat stipend at the end of the term instead of an hourly wage
choices.feedback: A stipend for regular work is a red flag. Someone doing the office's work is an employee, paid through payroll with at least minimum wage for every hour. Next time: hire a paid intern for her worker type, and pay her through payroll.

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: Dr. Park's office asked how to pay a spring intern a stipend for data entry. That's wages, so she has to be hired and paid through payroll.
consequences.summary: The internship was planned as a stipend for regular work.
consequences.task: Help Dr. Park set the intern up as a paid hire.

choices.text: No answer by Thursday
choices.feedback: With no answer from you, Dr. Park told the student the internship is unpaid, for work that points to an employee. Next time: answer within the week, and settle paid or unpaid before any offer.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: I never heard back about the intern, so I told her it's unpaid. Now Ravi says that's a problem.
consequences.summary: The internship went ahead as unpaid for regular work.

decisions.label: Setting her up
decisions.prompt: Dr. Park also wants the student set up in Oracle before the holidays, so her access is ready in January. What do you do first?

choices.text: Ask Ravi which worker type and checks fit an intern, then hire her that way
choices.feedback: A paid intern is hired like any worker of her type, and the type sets which checks apply. Which type Vanderbilt uses for interns is still being confirmed [SME], so Ravi's answer comes first. Next time: get the worker type from your EC before anyone builds a record.

choices.text: Add her as a non-worker affiliate with Active no payroll, so her access is ready
choices.feedback: Non-worker setup is only for people who won't be paid, and Active no payroll keeps her out of payroll entirely, so her hours would never pay. Next time: set up an intern who does the office's work as a paid worker of her type, confirmed with your EC.

consequences.speaker: ec_menon
consequences.line: The spring intern is set up as a non-worker with Active no payroll. She'd work all spring and never see a paycheck.
consequences.summary: The intern was set up as an unpaid non-worker.
consequences.task: Set the intern up for her worker type, with Ravi's guidance.

choices.text: Send her details to payroll and ask them to set her up before January
choices.feedback: Payroll pays what the hire record says, but it doesn't create hires. Setting up the hire is yours, once your EC confirms the worker type. Next time: confirm the worker type with your EC, then hire her through that process yourself.

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: I got a request to set up a spring intern. Payroll doesn't create hires, so that one's back with you.
consequences.summary: The intern's setup went to payroll and stalled.
consequences.task: Confirm the intern's worker type with Ravi, then set up the hire.

choices.text: Nothing set up by Thursday
choices.feedback: Nothing was set up, so the student's hire is still waiting. Next time: confirm the worker type with your EC early, so the hire is ready on time.

steps.title: A grad fellow's stipend
steps.context: Hannah Weiss, Research Finance, in chat: "It's a fellowship paid from our training grant. She doesn't do any work or services for the money. I need to know how it will be set up."

opener.speaker: fin_weiss
opener.line: Our grant pays a graduate fellow a $1,000 stipend this term, with no work attached. How will you set her up?

steps.hint: Does the fellow do any work for the money? Which setup fits a payment with no services?

decisions.prompt: How do you set up the fellow's stipend?

choices.text: Service free stipend, hire reason Service free appointment, no I-9
choices.feedback: Right. A student who gets a stipend and performs no services is a service free stipend: hire reason Service free appointment, with no I-9 and no background check. Its status, costing, and tax setup are still being confirmed, so check those with Ravi. Next time: if she's ever asked to work for the money, she becomes a student worker with an I-9.

choices.text: Hire her as a student worker paid by stipend, with an I-9 like any paid student
choices.feedback: She performs no services, so she isn't working for pay, and Service free appointment exists for exactly this case. Hiring her as a student worker misstates her record. Next time: work for pay is a student worker; a stipend with no work is a service free stipend.

choices.text: Student Expense Only, since the stipend isn't a wage for work
choices.feedback: Student Expense Only pays back expenses a student actually had. A $1,000 stipend isn't a reimbursement. Next time: a stipend with no services uses hire reason Service free appointment.

steps.title: A roster for Monday's org chart
steps.context: Dr. Park is presenting the office's org chart at a staff meeting on Mon Oct 26. Noor Haddad's first day is planned for that same day, and her hire is not final yet.

opener.speaker: dir_park
opener.line: Can you pull me a roster from Oracle with names, titles, and managers for Monday's org chart? Make sure Noor is on it.

steps.hint: Oracle keeps every change with a date. Which date is Dr. Park's chart about?

decisions.label: As-of date
decisions.prompt: The roster report asks for an as-of date. What do you enter?

choices.text: Mon Oct 26, the day she presents the chart
choices.feedback: Right. Oracle data is date effective, so a report shows what is in effect on its as-of date. A hire that starts Oct 26 appears only on a report run for Oct 26 or later [SME: which roster report HCMs run]. Next time: set the date prompt to the date the report is about.

choices.text: Today's date, for the most current data
choices.feedback: Today's date shows today's staff. Anyone who starts Monday is left off, even after their hire is final. Next time: set the as-of date to the date the report is about, not the day you run it.

consequences.speaker: new_haddad
consequences.line: My first day, and I was the only person in the room who wasn't on the org chart.
consequences.summary: Noor was left off Monday's org chart because the roster was run as of the wrong date.

choices.text: Sun Oct 25, the first day of the next pay period
choices.feedback: Oct 25 starts pay period 23, but Noor's first day is Oct 26. A report as of the 25th shows the office the day before she starts. Next time: use the exact date the report is about.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: Your roster was one day short. Noor started Monday and wasn't on my chart.
consequences.summary: The roster missed Noor because it was run as of the day before she started.

choices.text: No roster by Wednesday noon
choices.feedback: No roster came, so Dr. Park built the chart from an old list. Next time: run the report the day it is asked for, and rerun it when the data changes.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: I built the org chart from last year's list because the roster never came.
consequences.summary: Dr. Park's org chart was built from an outdated list.

decisions.label: Noor
decisions.prompt: Noor's hire isn't final yet, so the roster may not show her. What do you do?

spoken.speaker: dir_park
spoken.line: If Noor isn't in Oracle yet, just type her in. The chart can't miss her.

choices.text: Send it now, and rerun it as of Oct 26 once her hire is final
choices.feedback: Right. A report only shows what is in Oracle. Once Noor is converted and her hire is approved with an Oct 26 start, a rerun as of Oct 26 picks her up, and the chart matches the record [SME: whether pending workers show on roster reports]. Next time: tell the requester when the data will be final, and rerun then.

consequences.speaker: new_haddad
consequences.line: I was already on the org chart on my first day. It made me feel expected.
consequences.summary: Noor appeared on the org chart from a rerun after her hire was final.

choices.text: Type Noor into the exported roster so the chart is complete
choices.feedback: A typed-in name makes the roster disagree with Oracle, and files like this get reused long after Monday. If her start date moves, the list is wrong and nobody can tell. Next time: let Oracle be the source, and rerun once the hire is final.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: I used your roster to plan the grant budget, and it doesn't match Oracle. Which one is right?
consequences.summary: A hand-edited roster was reused for budgeting and didn't match Oracle.

choices.text: Add Noor in Oracle as a direct hire so she shows up
choices.feedback: Noor is already moving through recruiting, so a direct hire creates a second record for the same person. Duplicates split her history, pay, and costing, and central HR has to untangle them. Next time: ask central recruiting where a hire stands before you create anything.

consequences.speaker: new_haddad
consequences.line: I got two welcome emails with two different employee numbers. Which one is me?
consequences.summary: A duplicate record was created for Noor.
consequences.task: Ask central HR to remove Noor's duplicate record.

decisions.label: Saving the report
decisions.prompt: You trimmed the shared roster report to names, titles, and managers. How do you save it?

choices.text: Save As a copy in My Folders, and leave the shared one as is
choices.feedback: Right. Save As puts your version in My Folders, where only you can see it, and the shared report stays the same for everyone else. Your copy won't pick up later fixes to the original. Next time: check the shared original now and then.

choices.text: Save over the shared report so it's ready next time
choices.feedback: Saving over a shared report changes it for everyone who runs it, and their columns disappear without warning. Next time: use Save As and keep your version in My Folders.

consequences.speaker: coach
consequences.line: The roster report I run every Monday lost half its columns. Did you save over it?
consequences.summary: Saving over a shared report broke it for other users.
consequences.task: Restore the shared report and save your version in My Folders.

choices.text: Don't save it. Export the results and redo the edits next time
choices.feedback: Without a saved copy, you rebuild the same edits every time, and it's easy to miss a column or let an extra one in. Next time: Save As in My Folders, so the report is ready when you rerun it.

consequences.speaker: dir_park
consequences.line: Friday's version of the roster had home addresses on it. I only needed names and titles.
consequences.summary: Rebuilding the report by hand let personal data slip into the roster.

steps.title: Using an outside search firm
steps.context: Dr. Park plans to hire an associate director next year. She wants an outside search firm she has used before to run the search.

opener.speaker: dir_park
opener.line: Can you open a requisition so my search firm can get started?

steps.hint: How does an outside firm get paid, and who should hear about an executive search first?

decisions.prompt: How do you set up Dr. Park's search?

choices.text: Check with central recruiting first, then set up a PO requisition for the firm
choices.feedback: Outside firms are paid differently, so you bring one in through a PO requisition with your procurement contact, not a recruiting requisition. Next time: check with central recruiting before any executive search starts.

choices.text: Ask Tyler to open a recruiting requisition with the Executive search type
choices.feedback: The Executive search type is only for the recruiting partner's own executive search program, not an outside firm. Next time: an outside firm goes through a PO requisition, after you check with central recruiting.

choices.text: Open a Standard requisition, and have the firm send its candidates to it
choices.feedback: A Standard requisition runs the regular recruiting process, and it can't pay an outside firm. Next time: engage outside firms through a PO requisition, after you check with central recruiting.

steps.title: Lena's September costing
steps.context: Lena Kowalski is paid 50% from the Wellness grant and 50% from the department account. Mei Chen pulled Lena's costing History and found the first record keyed wrong. In this office you enter costing, using the account strings Mei sends.

opener.speaker: emp_chen
opener.line: Lena's September pay charged 100% to our department, and the grant should have paid half. Can we still fix it, or is September a lost cause?

attachment.title: Lena Kowalski: costing History
lines: From: Mei Chen
Subject: Lena's September costing
Record 1, Aug 30 to Sep 26 (pay periods 19 and 20): department account 100%
Record 2, Sep 27 onward: Wellness grant 50%, department account 50%
Record 1 should have been 50/50. The grant started paying half on Aug 30.
Calendar: Retro Change Cutoff is Wed Oct 21.

steps.hint: In the History, which record is wrong, and for how much of its range? Then check the calendar for the cutoff that applies to periods already paid.

decisions.label: Fix the record
decisions.prompt: Which change do you make to record 1 in Costing for Persons?

choices.text: Correct record 1 to 50/50, searching on Sun Aug 30
choices.feedback: Correct revises a record for its whole date range, so periods 19 and 20 now show 50/50 and record 2 stays as it is. You search on the first day of the period the costing should have started. Next time: read History first, then match the action to the problem.

choices.text: End Date record 1, searching on Sat Sep 26, its last day
choices.feedback: End Date stops costing from that date forward, so it would also end record 2, the correct split, and record 1 would still say 100% department. Next time: use Correct for a record that was wrong all along, and never End Date a past period you want to keep records after.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: Now Lena's October pay charged 100% to us too. The grant split is gone from her record.
consequences.summary: Lena's correct 50/50 record was ended by mistake, so this payroll charged the department in full.
consequences.task: Restore Lena's 50/50 costing from Sep 27 and send a retro form for every period charged wrong.

choices.text: Delete record 1, so the work unit default takes over
choices.feedback: With record 1 gone, those periods have no costing, and blank costing charges the work unit default, which is the department. The grant still pays nothing for September. Next time: blank means the default, so fix a wrong record with Correct.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: Lena's September still shows 100% on our account. The grant never picked up its half.
consequences.summary: Deleting the record left Lena's September charged to the department in full.
consequences.task: Correct Lena's Aug 30 costing to 50/50 and send the retro form.

choices.text: Not fixed
choices.feedback: Lena's costing wasn't fixed before the Retro Change Cutoff. Next time: fix past costing the day it's found.

decisions.label: Paid periods
decisions.prompt: Periods 19 and 20 were paid weeks ago. What else has to happen for the grant to pick up its half?

choices.text: Send the Retro Costing Request Form to Research Finance
choices.feedback: Periods already paid need the Retro Costing Request Form (Salary), sent to Research Finance by the Retro Change Cutoff, Wed Oct 21, showing the costing as it should have been. If the Wellness grant is externally funded, add a cost transfer memo [SME: ask Mei]. Next time: fix the record and send the form the same day.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: Research Finance moved half of Lena's September pay to the grant. Thank you for beating the cutoff.
consequences.summary: Lena's September costing was corrected through the retro form.

choices.text: Email payroll to run retro costing for periods 19 and 20
choices.feedback: Retro costing requests go to Research Finance on the Retro Costing Request Form, not to payroll by email, and HCMs never ask payroll to rerun a paid period. Next time: send the form by the Retro Change Cutoff; that is the request finance acts on.

consequences.speaker: pay_liu
consequences.line: We don't take costing fixes by email. Lena's September needs the retro costing form, and Wednesday's cutoff has passed.
consequences.summary: Lena's retro costing missed the Retro Change Cutoff while sitting in payroll's inbox.
consequences.task: Send Lena's Retro Costing Request Form by the next Retro Change Cutoff.

choices.text: Nothing more; the fixed record reposts past charges
choices.feedback: A record fix alone isn't enough for periods that were already paid. Vanderbilt also needs the Retro Costing Request Form at Research Finance by the Retro Change Cutoff. Next time: any change that reaches a paid period gets the form.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: Your fix shows in Oracle, but September is still sitting on our budget. Did the retro form ever go in?
consequences.summary: No retro form was sent, so Lena's September pay stayed on the department budget.
consequences.task: Send Lena's Retro Costing Request Form by the next Retro Change Cutoff.

choices.text: Form not sent by the Retro Change Cutoff
choices.feedback: The form didn't reach Research Finance by the Retro Change Cutoff, Wed Oct 21, so the fix waits for the next cycle [SME]. Next time: send past period fixes the day you find them.

consequences.speaker: emp_chen
consequences.line: We missed Wednesday's cutoff, so Lena's September fix waits another cycle. Now I have to explain that to Dana.
consequences.summary: Lena's retro costing missed the Retro Change Cutoff.
consequences.task: Send Lena's Retro Costing Request Form by the next Retro Change Cutoff.

steps.title: Search shows 4 Kowalskis
steps.context: Mei's costing question means opening Lena Kowalski's record. Your name search for Kowalski returns 4 people across campus.

opener.speaker: coach
opener.line: Four Kowalskis came back. How do you make sure you open the right one?

steps.hint: Names and titles repeat across campus. What does Oracle give each person that never repeats?

decisions.prompt: How do you find Lena's record?

choices.text: Search by her person number, then check her type and status
choices.feedback: Right. The person number is unique and safe to use. Check the person type and status in the results, and make sure you're on the right assignment before you act. Next time: start every lookup with the person number.

choices.text: Search by her SSN instead, since no two people ever share one

choices.text: Open the Kowalski whose job title says Data Assistant
choices.feedback: Titles repeat across campus, so a title match can still land on the wrong person. One wrong click and your change goes on someone else's record. Next time: search by person number and confirm type and status.

choices.text: Hold off until she sets up a business, then pay her invoices

steps.title: A termination for misconduct

choices.text: Not yet; first Ravi and leadership settle access and rehire
choices.feedback: Misconduct exits carry legal and security risk, so your EC and leadership decide when access ends and how the rehire field is marked [SME: field name] before anything is entered. Next time: after that talk, enter Involuntary termination with the reason Misconduct.
